passages.text: From the stands, the track was a strip of red between two lines of white. The crowd was loud, flags and hands and voices all moving at once. Then the gun cracked and the runners burst forward. Ayo was in lane three. She could not hear the crowd anymore. All she could hear was her own breathing, hard and fast, and the slap of her spikes against the rubber. The girl in lane four was pulling ahead. Ayo’s lungs burned. She leaned forward and found something she did not know she had. In the stands, her father had stopped clapping and was simply watching, his hands frozen in front of his chest, his mouth slightly open.
passages.label: Extract A — The Sports Day

passages.text: The photograph had been taken in 1974. Nasreen could tell from the colour — that washed-out orange that old film stock turns to, as though time itself were a kind of stain. Three women stood in front of a bus stop, squinting into the sun. The woman on the left was her grandmother, though Nasreen would never have recognised her without being told. She looked young, careless, her hair blown sideways by a wind that had stopped blowing fifty years ago. Nasreen turned the photograph over. On the back, in pencil so faint it was almost gone: Lahore, March. We leave tomorrow. She turned it back. Her grandmother’s face was still smiling. She had no idea what was coming.
passages.label: Extract B — The Photograph

passages.text: The first lightning strike hit the ridge at quarter past two. From the village below it looked like a crack in the sky, white and sudden and wrong, as though the air itself had broken. In the schoolhouse, the children pressed their faces to the glass and counted the seconds between flash and thunder. Miss Parry told them to sit down. On the ridge, Gethin crouched behind a wall that was no longer keeping anything out. Rain came at him sideways, filling his eyes, his mouth, the space between his collar and his neck. He could not see the village. He could not see anything except the grass flattened by wind and the shape of his own hands. Below him, in the warm schoolhouse, his daughter was counting. One, two, three, four. She did not know the ridge was where her father worked.
passages.label: Extract C — The Storm

steps: Track where the writer’s ‘camera’ points: wide shot, close-up, internal thought?
Identify any shifts: does focus move from one character to another? From setting to thought?
Note time shifts: flashback, flash-forward, or real-time?
Explain why the shift happens at that point — what does it reveal or conceal?
Link to reader experience: tension, surprise, sympathy, understanding
method_card.title: Structural Analysis: Focus and Perspective Shifts
method_card.content: Writers control what the reader focuses on and whose perspective they experience. Shifts in focus (wide to narrow, external to internal, present to past) and perspective (one character to another, or from action to thought) are deliberate structural choices that shape meaning and reader engagement.

exam_context.marks: 8 marks — how does the writer structure the text to interest you as a reader?
exam_context.paper: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing
exam_context.frequency: Every Paper 1 exam. Focus shifts are one of the most common structural features to analyse.

gold.context: A good response analyses the alternating structure: village → schoolhouse → ridge → schoolhouse. Each shift changes perspective (children, Gethin, daughter) and creates dramatic irony. The reader knows Gethin is in danger; his daughter does not. Should discuss how the parallel structure (father on the ridge, daughter counting in the schoolhouse) creates emotional tension through juxtaposition.
gold.question: How does the writer use shifts in focus and perspective to create tension in this passage? Analyse the structural choices in detail.

claims: Wide establishing shot that sets the scene for the reader
Shift to an enclosed, safe interior — creating contrast with the danger outside
Close focus on one person’s physical vulnerability
Dramatic irony created by a character’s ignorance

In the schoolhouse, the children pressed their faces to the glass and counted the seconds

gold.question: Match each structural function to the part of the text that performs it.
This analysis contains some accurate and some inaccurate points. Click on the misinterpretations.

summaryParts.text: The writer alternates between two locations — the schoolhouse and the ridge — to create a structural parallel between father and daughter.
The shift to Gethin on the ridge reduces tension because the reader can see he is safe behind the wall.
summaryParts.explain: The wall is described as “no longer keeping anything out” — it offers no protection. The shift to Gethin increases tension by showing how exposed and vulnerable he is.

summaryParts.text: The daughter counting seconds structurally mirrors the opening’s description of the lightning, connecting her innocently to her father’s danger without her knowing it.
The final sentence creates dramatic irony: the daughter does not know her father is on the ridge, but the reader does.
The alternating structure between safety and danger creates no emotional effect because the scenes are unrelated.
summaryParts.explain: The scenes are deeply connected — father and daughter are linked by the storm. The structural juxtaposition between the warm schoolhouse and the exposed ridge intensifies both settings through contrast.

gold.context: A good response evaluates how the dual perspective creates dramatic irony and emotional tension that a single viewpoint could not achieve. If we only saw Gethin, we would feel his danger but not the poignancy of his daughter counting innocently. If we only saw the daughter, we would not feel the physical threat. The alternation forces the reader to hold both realities simultaneously. Should consider the structural impact of the final sentence revealing the family connection.
gold.question: To what extent does the writer’s use of alternating perspectives create a more powerful emotional effect than a single perspective would? Evaluate with reference to specific structural choices.

gold.context: A good response identifies that counting appears in both locations: the children count seconds between flash and thunder, and the daughter counts at the end (“One, two, three, four”). But the counting has different meaning in each context: for the children it is a game; for the reader, knowing Gethin is on the ridge, it becomes a measure of proximity to danger. This structural echo creates ironic resonance between the two perspectives.
gold.question: Analyse how the writer uses the motif of counting to connect the schoolhouse and the ridge structurally.

bronze.question: Classify each structural shift in the extract.

statements.text: The focus moves from the stands to Ayo’s internal experience.
statements.explain: The writer narrows from a panoramic crowd view to the private world inside Ayo’s head.

statements.text: The final sentence moves back to Ayo’s father in the stands.
statements.explain: After being inside Ayo’s experience, the focus pulls back to the stands to show her father’s reaction.

statements.text: The passage shifts from what Ayo can hear (everything) to what she cannot hear (the crowd).
statements.explain: The crowd noise disappears as focus moves inward — a structural choice that reflects Ayo’s tunnel vision.

statements.text: The focus briefly moves to the girl in lane four pulling ahead.
statements.explain: The rival is the only external detail Ayo registers during the internal section — because she is the competitive threat.

bronze.question: Highlight the sentence where the focus shifts from the crowd to Ayo’s internal experience.
bronze.answer_text: She could not hear the crowd anymore.
bronze.explanation: This sentence marks the transition. The crowd — dominant in the opening — disappears, and the reader enters Ayo’s private sensory world.

bronze.question: The passage ends with Ayo’s father: “his hands frozen in front of his chest, his mouth slightly open.” What effects does this shift to his perspective create?

options: To provide factual information about the race layout
To act as a pivot point that shifts the focus from external to internal

bronze.question: Why does the writer place “Ayo was in lane three” as a short sentence between the crowd description and her internal experience?
Highlight the phrase where Ayo becomes aware of an external threat during her internal focus.
bronze.answer_text: The girl in lane four was pulling ahead.
bronze.explanation: This is the only detail from outside Ayo’s body that penetrates her internal focus. Structurally, it introduces the competitive pressure that drives the next moment.

bronze.question: Is each statement about the structural shifts accurate or inaccurate?

statements.text: The opening wide-angle view makes the reader feel they are watching from the stands.
statements.explain: The perspective mirrors a spectator’s view: the track as a strip, flags and voices.

statements.text: The shift to Ayo’s perspective makes the race feel slower and more relaxed.
statements.explain: The internal focus makes the race feel more intense, not relaxed. We experience Ayo’s burning lungs and hard breathing.

statements.text: The return to the father at the end creates a sense of two people connected by the same moment but experiencing it differently.
statements.explain: Ayo is inside the race; her father watches from outside. Same moment, different experiences — this dual perspective adds depth.

Perspective shift — moving from the photograph’s surface to its hidden message

silver.question: Match each structural technique to the quotation that demonstrates it.
Read this structural analysis. Click on the parts that misinterpret the text.

summaryParts.text: The writer structures the passage around a photograph, using it as a device to move between present and past.
Nasreen recognises her grandmother immediately, which creates a strong emotional connection from the start.
summaryParts.explain: The text says Nasreen “would never have recognised her without being told.” The inability to recognise her own grandmother emphasises the distance between past and present, not immediate connection.

summaryParts.text: The phrase “a wind that had stopped blowing fifty years ago” merges two time frames, making the photograph feel alive and dead at the same time.
The message on the back (“We leave tomorrow”) adds a layer of narrative that the image alone cannot convey, shifting focus from visual to verbal.
The ending is happy because the grandmother is smiling, showing she had a good life after the photograph.
summaryParts.explain: The ending is poignant, not happy. “She had no idea what was coming” implies upheaval or difficulty ahead. The smile is painful precisely because it belongs to someone unaware of their future.

chips.text: Dramatic irony — the reader and Nasreen know more than the grandmother
It makes the earlier smile feel poignant rather than happy
It resolves all the mystery in the passage
It creates a gap between the grandmother’s present (1974) and Nasreen’s present
It confirms the grandmother had an easy life
It leaves the reader with a sense of unease about what happened next

silver.question: The writer ends with “She had no idea what was coming.” What effects does placing this as the final sentence create?

silver.quote: her hair blown sideways by a wind that had stopped blowing fifty years ago
silver.context: A good response analyses how the writer moves between time frames: Nasreen’s present, the 1974 photograph, and the gap between them. Should discuss the phrase about the wind (which collapses time) and the ending (which exploits the knowledge gap). The physical act of turning the photograph over is a structural pivot — moving from image to text, surface to hidden meaning.
silver.question: How does the writer use shifts between past and present to create meaning in this extract? Analyse specific structural choices.
Highlight the physical action that marks a structural shift from the photograph’s surface to its hidden information.
silver.explanation: This simple action shifts the focus from visual (the image) to textual (the pencilled note). It’s a structural pivot: the front of the photo shows what can be seen; the back reveals what was felt.

silver.question: Classify each structural observation as accurate or inaccurate.

statements.text: The passage uses the photograph as a framing device to move between two time periods.
statements.explain: The photograph anchors both 1974 (the image) and the present (Nasreen examining it), allowing the writer to shift between them.

statements.text: The colour description (“washed-out orange”) serves no structural purpose.
statements.explain: It establishes the time gap immediately — the faded colour is physical evidence of the distance between past and present.

statements.text: The ending creates dramatic irony because Nasreen knows her grandmother’s future but the photograph captures a moment of ignorance.
statements.explain: The knowledge gap between Nasreen and her frozen grandmother is the source of the passage’s emotional power.

statements.text: The pencilled note shifts the register from visual description to something more intimate and urgent.
statements.explain: “We leave tomorrow” introduces voices, plans, and implied upheaval — a shift from observing to understanding.

options: It describes the weather in Lahore in 1974
It merges past and present in a single image, highlighting the distance between them
It shows that Nasreen is imagining things
It proves the photograph is fake
silver.question: What is the main structural effect of the phrase “a wind that had stopped blowing fifty years ago”?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: The passage begins with a wide-angle view from the stands: the track, the crowd, the noise. This establishes the public spectacle.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: After “Ayo was in lane three,” the focus narrows sharply into her internal experience. The crowd disappears: “She could not hear the crowd anymore.”

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: This shift from external/public to internal/private puts the reader inside Ayo’s head. We experience the race as she does — breathing, burning lungs, the rival pulling ahead.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer shifts from a wide, external view of the sports day to Ayo’s intense internal experience. The crowd’s noise vanishes as focus narrows to her breathing and physical sensation. This structural zoom-in creates intimacy and tension — the reader feels trapped inside the race with her.

worked_examples.passage: From the stands, the track was a strip of red between two lines of white. The crowd was loud, flags and hands and voices all moving at once. Then the gun cracked and the runners burst forward. Ayo was in lane three. She could not hear the crowd anymore.
worked_examples.question: How does the writer use a shift in focus to create tension during the race?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: The passage operates in two time frames: Nasreen in the present, looking at the photograph, and the women in 1974. The writer moves between these throughout.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: The phrase “a wind that had stopped blowing fifty years ago” is key. It collapses the two time frames into one sentence — the wind is present in the image but gone in reality.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: The ending intensifies this: “She had no idea what was coming.” Nasreen, in the present, knows the grandmother’s future. The grandmother, frozen in 1974, does not. This gap in knowledge creates dramatic irony and poignancy.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer structures the passage around a time shift between present (Nasreen examining the photo) and past (1974). The structural tension comes from the knowledge gap: Nasreen knows what happened after the photo was taken, but the grandmother “had no idea.” This dramatic irony makes the smiling face poignant rather than happy, because the reader shares Nasreen’s awareness of what is to come.

worked_examples.passage: She looked young, careless, her hair blown sideways by a wind that had stopped blowing fifty years ago.

ai_marking_prompts.evaluation:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor. The student is evaluating how a writer uses structural techniques including focus and perspective shifts. Mark their response using these levels:

- Mastering (excellent): Takes a clear evaluative position; analyses HOW alternating perspectives or focus shifts create effects that a single perspective could not; considers the relationship between structure and emotional impact; sophisticated.
- Secure (good): Evaluates with evidence and some analysis of structural effect; clear personal response; mostly convincing.
- Developing (needs_work): Some evaluation attempted but limited analysis of structural choices; may describe events rather than evaluate the effect of perspective shifts.
- Emerging (not_valid): Retells or describes without evaluating; no personal position; no analysis of focus or perspective.

Be encouraging. Reward insight over format. Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional brief tip"}
ai_marking_prompts.structure_analysis:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor. The student is analysing how a writer uses focus shifts and perspective changes to structure a text. Mark their response using these levels:

- Mastering (excellent): Identifies specific shifts in focus, perspective, or time; explains how the structural choices create effects (tension, irony, sympathy, contrast); considers how the ordering of perspectives shapes the reader’s experience; perceptive.
- Secure (good): Identifies structural shifts and explains some effects; references specific parts of the text; links structure to meaning.
- Developing (needs_work): Identifies that the focus changes but explanation is vague; may describe what happens rather than analyse why the shift matters.
- Emerging (not_valid): Retells the story without reference to structural shifts; no analysis of how focus or perspective is used.

Be encouraging. Reward genuine insight even if imperfectly expressed. Do NOT require PEE structure. Accept paraphrased evidence. Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional brief tip"}
